title: Why Are Train Wheels Shaped Like Cones?
description:
A train has no steering wheel. Its wheels are fixed to a solid steel axle, so both wheels always turn at exactly the same speed. And yet a train can go around a curve at three hundred kilometers an hour without grinding itself apart. The secret is a shape most people never notice. Train wheels are not flat cylinders. They are cones. Today, ten parts of a railway, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:10 1. The cone-shaped wheel
2:31 2. The flange
3:48 3. The solid axle
5:14 4. The tilted rail
6:35 5. The bogie
7:56 6. The rail without gaps
9:24 7. The sandbox
10:48 8. The hammer test
12:13 9. The knuckle coupler
13:39 10. The air brake hose
15:10 The verdict

Sources:
- Conical wheels, self-steering and hunting oscillation (Klingel, 1883): Wikipedia, "Hunting oscillation" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting_oscillation and "Wheelset (rail transport)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelset_(rail_transport)
- Richard Feynman on conical train wheels: BBC "Fun to Imagine" (1983)
- Flange, rail profile and rail inclination (1 in 20 / 1 in 40): Wikipedia, "Rail profile" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_profile
- Bogies and John B. Jervis: Wikipedia, "Bogie" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogie and "John B. Jervis" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_B._Jervis
- Jacobs bogies on the TGV: Wikipedia, "Jacobs bogie" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobs_bogie
- Continuous welded rail, neutral temperature and sun kinks: Wikipedia, "Track (rail transport)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_(rail_transport) and US FRA, "Track buckling prevention" https://railroads.dot.gov/
- Leaf fall and railhead treatment: Network Rail, "Leaves on the line" https://www.networkrail.co.uk/running-the-railway/looking-after-the-railway/delays-explained/leaves/
- Wheel tappers: Wikipedia, "Wheeltapper" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeltapper
- Eschede derailment (3 June 1998, 101 deaths): Wikipedia, "Eschede train disaster" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eschede_train_disaster
- Janney knuckle coupler (1873) and the Safety Appliance Act (1893): Wikipedia, "Railway coupling" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_coupling and "Safety Appliance Act" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_Appliance_Act
- Westinghouse automatic air brake: Wikipedia, "Railway air brake" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_air_brake
